body.heading: The same answer, everywhere
paragraphs: In India, Diwali fills streets and windows with oil lamps and candles, celebrating the victory of light over darkness. In Jewish homes, Hanukkah adds a candle each night for eight nights, remembering a small jar of oil that burned far longer than it should have.

In Sweden, St Lucia's Day brings a candlelit procession on one of the darkest mornings of the year. In Thailand, Yi Peng releases thousands of lanterns into the night sky, while Loi Krathong floats small decorated baskets on the water.

body.heading: Why light, why then
paragraphs: Many of these festivals gather in the darkest part of the year in the northern hemisphere, and that is no coincidence. Lighting a lamp together is a way of saying the dark is real — and so is our answer to it.

You do not need to belong to a tradition to learn from its shape: mark the season, gather your people, and put actual light in an actual window. Traditions travel best when they are borrowed respectfully and credited honestly.
